{{wp}}

===Pronunciation===

* {{a|en|UK}}
** {{IPA|en|/fɔːl/|a=RP}}
** {{IPA|en|/foːl/|a=SSBE}}
** {{IPA|en|/fɔl/|a=Scotland}}
** {{IPA|en|/faːl/|a=Northumbrian}}
* {{a|en|US}}
** {{IPA|en|/fɔl/|a=non-cot-caught}}
** {{IPA|en|/fɑl/|a=cot-caught}}
**: {{audio|en|En-us-fall.ogg|a=California}}

===Etymology 1===
Verb from {{inh|en|enm|fallen}}, from {{inh|en|ang|feallan|t=to fall, fail, decay, die, attack}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*fallan|t=to fall}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*fallaną|t=to fall}}, from {{inh|en|ine-pro|*h₃elh₁-|t=to collapse, fall; to destroy}}.
{{col-top|2|cog}}
Cognate with {{cog|sco|faw|t=to fall}}, {{cog|yol|vale}}, {{m|yol|vall}}, {{m|yol|vole|t=to fall}}, {{cog|frr|faal}}, {{m|frr|fåle|t=to fall}}, {{cog|stq|faale|t=to fall}}, {{cog|fy|falle|t=to fall}}, {{cog|bar|foin|t=to fall}}, {{cog|cim|ballan}}, {{m|cim|vallan|t=to fall}}, {{cog|nl|vallen|t=to fall}}, {{cog|de,nds|fallen|t=to fall}}, {{cog|lb|falen|t=to fall}}, {{cog|yi|פֿאַלן|t=to fall}}, {{cog|da|falde|t=to fall}}, {{cog|fo,is,sv|falla|t=to fall}}, {{cog|nb|falle|t=to fall}}, {{cog|nn|falla}}, {{m|nn|falle|t=to fall}}; also {{cog|la|aboleō|t=to destroy; to die}}, {{cog|grc|ὄλλῡμι|t=to destroy; to lose}}, {{cog|hy|եղեռն|t=crime; calamity, catastrophe; slaughter}}, {{cog|lt|pùlti|t=to fall; to attack, assault}}.

Noun from {{inh|en|enm|fal}}, {{m|enm|fall}}, {{m|enm|falle}}, from {{inh|en|ang|feall}}, {{m|ang|ġefeall|t=a falling, fall}} and {{inh|en|ang|fealle|t=trap, snare}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*fallą}}, {{m|gem-pro|*fallaz|t=a fall, trap}}. Cognate with {{cog|yol|vall|t=fall}}, {{cog|nl|val|t=fall}}, {{cog|de|Fall|t=fall}}, {{cog|da|fald|t=fall}}, {{cog|fo,is,nb,nn,sv|fall|t=fall}}.
{{col-bottom}}

Sense of "autumn" is attested by the 1660s in [[England]] as a shortening of ''[[fall of the leaf]]'' (1540s), from the falling of leaves during this season. Along with ''autumn'', it mostly replaced the older name ''[[harvest]]'' as that name began to be associated strictly with the act of harvesting. Compare ''[[spring]]'', which began as a shortening of “spring of the leaf”.

====Alternative forms====
* {{alter|en|fal||obsolete}}

====Verb====
{{en-verb|~s|~ing|fell|~en}}
[[File:Vienna Convention road sign Aa-11a-V1.svg|thumb|A sign warning about the danger of '''falling''' rocks.]]

# {{lb|en|heading|intransitive}} ''To be moved downwards.''
## To move to a lower position under the effect of [[gravity]].
##: {{ux|en|Thrown from a cliff, the stone '''fell''' 100 feet before hitting the ground.}}
##: {{ux|en|I '''fell''' unconscious on the floor.}}
##* {{RQ:Belloc Lowndes Lodger|II|0091
|passage=There was a neat hat-and-umbrella stand, and the stranger's weary feet '''fell''' soft on a good, serviceable dark-red drugget, which matched in colour the flock-paper on the walls.}}
## To come down, to [[drop]] or [[descend]].
##: {{ux|en|The rain '''fell''' at dawn.}}
##* {{quote-book|en|year=1920|author=w:Herman Cyril McNeile|title=w:Bulldog Drummond|chapter=1
|passage=Her eyes '''fell''' on the table, and she advanced into the room wiping her hands on her apron.}}
##* {{RQ:en:CNN|author=Rory Smith|title=IQ scores are falling and have been for decades, new study finds|url=https://www.cnn.com/2018/06/13/health/falling-iq-scores-study-intl|date=2018-06-13|passage=The study not only showed IQ variance between children the same parents, but because the authors had the IQ scores of various parents, it demonstrated that parents with higher IQs tended to have more kids, ruling out the dysgenic fertility theory as a driver of '''falling''' IQ scores and highlighting the role of environmental factors instead.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20260402133215/https://www.cnn.com/2018/06/13/health/falling-iq-scores-study-intl|archivedate=2 April 2026}}
## To come as if by dropping down.
##* {{quote-book|en|year=1898|author=William Le Queux|title=Whoso Findeth a Wife|page=256
|passage=Once or twice a noise '''fell''' upon his quick ear, and we halted, he standing revolver in hand in an attitude of defense. Each time, however, we ascertained that we had no occasion for alarm, the noise being made by some animal or bird  ...}}
##* {{quote-book|en|year=1904|author=Bram Stoker|title=The Jewel of Seven Stars|page=248
|passage=And then a sudden calm '''fell''' on us like a cloud of fear. There! on the table, lay the Jewel of Seven Stars, shining and sparkling with lurid light, as though each of the seven points of each of the seven stars gleamed through blood!}}
##*: Shortly afterwards a breeze came up from the N {{...}} dark clouds closing in over everything. At 3 in the afternoon the breeze came up from the S with a thick drizzle. Thus night '''fell''', and thus we passed the rest of it.
##* {{quote-book|en|year=1981|author=Dan Kirby|title=Schreiber's Choice|publisher=Ace Books|isbn=9780441761982
|passage=The horse wrangler, a tall, bronzed-face man, waved to the wagon driver. The driver laughed. {{...}} The canvas cover rolled up suddenly and a terrible noise '''fell''' over the desert.}}
## To come to the ground [[deliberately]], to [[prostrate]] oneself.
##: {{ux|en|He '''fell''' to the floor and begged for mercy.}}
## To be brought to the ground.
# {{lb|en|transitive}} ''To move downwards.''
## {{lb|en|obsolete}} To let fall; to drop.
##* {{RQ:Shakespeare Lucrece|passage=For every tear he '''falls''', a Trojan bleeds.}}
##* {{RQ:Shakespeare Richard 3|V|3|text=''Ghoaſt [of Clarence].'' {{...}} / To morrow in the battaile thinke on me, / And '''fall''' thy edgeleſſe ſword, diſpaire and die.}}
## {{lb|en|obsolete}} To sink; to depress.
##: {{ux|en|to '''fall''' the voice}}
## {{lb|en|UK|US|dialect|archaic}} To [[fell]]; to cut down.
##: {{ux|en|to '''fall''' a tree}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} ''To change, often negatively.''
## {{senseid|en|become}} {{lb|en|copulative|in idiomatic expressions}} To {{l|en|become|id=copulative}} {{q|chiefly used with negative states}}.
##: {{par|en|become<id:copulative>|get<id:become>|go<id:become>|turn<id:become>|come<id:become>|grow<id:become>|wax<id:become>}}
##: {{uxi|en|She has [[fall ill|'''fallen''' ill]].}}
##: {{uxi|en|The children [[fall asleep|'''fell''' asleep]] in the back of the car.}}
##: {{uxi|en|When did you first [[fall in love|'''fall''' in love]]?}}
##: {{uxi|en|[[fall silent|'''fall''' silent]], [[fall sick|'''fall''' sick]], [[fall pregnant|'''fall''' pregnant]], [[fall victim|'''fall''' victim]] to something}}
##* {{RQ:Dickens Little Dorrit|1|27|passage=At length they stood at the corner from which they had begun, and it had '''fallen''' quite dark, and they were no wiser.}}
##*: Shortly afterwards a breeze came up from the N and then it '''fell''' calm, {{...}}
## {{lb|en|intransitive}} To [[collapse]]; to be [[overthrown]] or [[defeated]].
##: {{ux|en|Rome '''fell''' to the Goths in 410 AD.}}
## {{lb|en|intransitive|formal|euphemistic}} To [[die]], especially in [[battle]] or by [[disease]].
##: {{ux|en|This is a monument to all those who '''fell''' in the First World War.}}
## {{lb|en|intransitive}} To become lower (in quantity, pitch, etc.).
##: {{ux|en|The candidate's poll ratings '''fell''' abruptly after the banking scandal.}}
##* {{quote-book|en|year=1612|author={{w|John Davies (poet)|John Davies}}|title=Discoverie of the True Causes why Ireland was never entirely subdued
|passage=The greatness of these Irish lords suddenly '''fell''' and vanished.}}
##* {{quote-book|en|year=1835|author=Sir {{w|John Ross (Arctic explorer)|John Ross}}; Sir {{w|James Clark Ross}}|title=[http://books.google.com.au/books?id=SdQBAAAAYAAJ Narrative of a Second Voyage in Search of a North-west Passage …, Vol.1]|pages=284–5
|passage=Towards the following morning, the thermometer '''fell''' to 5°; and at daylight, there was not an atom of water to be seen in any direction.}}
##* {{RQ:Economist|date=2013-07-20|volume=408|issue=8845|url=http://www.economist.com/news/science-and-technology/21581980-latest-research-suggests-humans-are-not-warriors-their-genes-after-all-old|title=Old soldiers?| passage=Whether modern, industrial man is less or more warlike than his hunter-gatherer ancestors is impossible to determine.{{...}}One thing that is true, though, is that murder rates have '''fallen''' over the centuries, as policing has spread and the routine carrying of weapons has diminished. Modern society may not have done anything about war. But peace is a lot more peaceful.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130822003848/http://www.economist.com/news/science-and-technology/21581980-latest-research-suggests-humans-are-not-warriors-their-genes-after-all-old}}
# {{senseid|en|occur}} To [[occur]] (on a certain day of the week, date, or similar); to [[happen]].
#: {{ux|en|Thanksgiving always '''falls''' on a Thursday.}}
#: {{ux|en|Last year, Commencement '''fell''' on June 3.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1978|author=Dwight David Eisenhower; Mamie Doud Eisenhower|title=Letters to Mamie|publisher=Doubleday Books
|passage=(Thus D-day '''fell''' on June 6 rather than the planned June 5.)}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To be [[allot]]ted to; to [[arrive]] through [[chance]], [[fate]], or [[inheritance]].
#: {{ux|en|And so it '''falls''' to me to make this important decision.}}
#: {{ux|en|The estate '''fell''' to his brother.}}
#: {{ux|en|The kingdom '''fell''' into the hands of his rivals.}}
#* {{RQ:Pope Rape of the Lock|year=1912|canto=II|passage=If to her share some female errors '''fall''', / Look on her face, and you'll forget them all.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|obsolete}} To diminish; to lessen or lower.
#* {{RQ:Locke Value|passage=Upon lessening interest to four per cent, you '''fall''' the price of your native commodities.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|obsolete}} To bring forth.
#: {{ux|en|to '''fall''' lambs}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Merchant of Venice|1|3|passage=The shepherd{{...}}did{{...}} '''fall''' part-colour'd lambs}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive|obsolete}} To issue forth into life; to be brought forth; said of the young of certain animals.
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To descend in character or [[reputation]]; to become degraded; to sink into [[vice]], [[error]]{{,}} or [[sin]].
#* {{RQ:KJV|Hebrews|4|1|text=Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man '''fall''' after the same example of unbelief.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To become ensnared or entrapped; to be worse off than before.
#: {{ux|en|to '''fall''' into error;  to '''fall''' into difficulties;  to '''fall''' into ruin}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To assume a look of shame or disappointment; to become or appear dejected; said of the face.
#* {{RQ:KJV|Genesis|4|5|text=Cain was very wroth, and his countenance '''fell'''.}}
#* {{RQ:Addison Cato|8|scene=iv|text=I have observed of late thy looks are '''fallen'''.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To happen; to come to pass; to chance or light (upon).
#* {{RQ:KJV|Ruth|3|18|text=Sit still, my daughter, until thou know how the matter will '''fall'''.}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Merchant of Venice|I|2|text={{...}}An the worst '''fall''' that ever '''fell''', I hope I shall make shift to go without him.}}
#* {{RQ:Swift Nobles and Commons|page=9|passage={{...}} ''{{w|Polybius}}'' tells us, the beſt Government is that which conſiſts of three Forms, ''Regno'', ''Optimatium'', & ''Populi imperio''. Which may be fairly Tranſlated, the ''Kings'', ''Lords'' and ''Commons''. {{...}} the ''Romans'' '''fell''' upon this Model purely by chance, (which I take to have been Nature and common Reaſon) but the ''Spartans'' by Thought and Deſign.}}
#* '''1879''', {{w|Herbert Spencer}}, ''Principles of Sociology'' Volume II – Part IV: ''Ceremonial Institutions''
#*: Primitive men{{...}}do not make laws, they '''fall''' into customs.
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To begin with haste, ardour, or vehemence; to rush or hurry.
#: {{ux|en|After arguing, they '''fell''' to blows.}}
#* '''1881''', {{w|Benjamin Jowett}} ({{w|Thucydides}})
#*: They now no longer doubted, but '''fell''' to work heart and soul.
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To be dropped or uttered carelessly.
#: {{ux|en|An unguarded expression '''fell''' from his lips.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive|of a fabric}} To [[hang]] down {{gloss|under the influence of gravity}}.
#: {{ux|en|An Empire-style dress has a high waistline – directly under the bust – from which the dress '''falls''' all the way to a hem as low as the floor.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive|slang|AAVE}} To visit; to go to a place.
#: {{ux|en|We'll '''fall''' over to the club tonight.}}

=====Synonyms=====
* {{sense|move to a lower position under the effect of gravity}} {{l|en|drop}}, {{l|en|plummet}}, {{l|en|plunge}}
* {{sense|come down}} {{l|en|come down}}, {{l|en|descend}}, {{l|en|drop}}
* {{sense|come to the ground deliberately}} {{l|en|drop}}, {{l|en|lower}} oneself, [[prostrate]] oneself
* {{sense|be brought to the ground}}
* {{qualifier|collapse; be overthrown or defeated}}: be [[beat]]en by, be [[defeat]]ed by, be [[overthrow]]n by, be [[smite|smitten]] by, be [[vanquish]]ed by,
* {{sense|die}} {{l|en|die}}
* {{sense|be allotted to}} be the [[responsibility]] of, be [[up to]]
* {{qualifier|become lower (in quantity, pitch, etc)}}: [[dip]], [[drop]]
* {{sense|become}} {{l|en|become}}, {{l|en|get}}
* {{qualifier|cause (something) to descend to the ground}}: [[cut down]] {{qualifier|of a tree}}, [[fell]], [[knock down]], [[knock over]], [[strike down]]

=====Antonyms=====
* {{antsense|come down}} {{l|en|ascend}}, {{l|en|go}} up, [[rise]]
* {{antsense|come to the ground deliberately}} {{l|en|get up}}, {{l|en|pick up|pick oneself up}}, {{l|en|stand up}}
* {{qualifier|collapse; be overthrown or defeated}}: [[beat]], [[defeat]], [[overthrow]], [[smite]], [[vanquish]]
* {{qualifier|become lower (in quantity, pitch, etc)}}: [[rise]]

|passage=“I'm through with all pawn-games,” I laughed. “Come, let us have a game of lansquenet. Either I will take a farewell '''fall''' out of you or you will have your sevenfold revenge”.}}
# {{senseid|en|autumn}}{{lb|en|chiefly|North America|archaic in Britain}} The time of the year when the [[leaves]] typically fall from the trees; [[autumn]]; the season of the year between the autumnal [[equinox]] and the winter [[solstice]]. {{defdate|from 16th c.}}
# A [[waterfall]].

# That which falls or cascades.

## {{lb|en|cricket|of a [[wicket]]}} The action of a [[batsman]] being [[out]].

=====Usage notes=====
* The phrase {{m|en|have a fall}}, as opposed to {{m|en|fall over}} or {{m|en|fall down}}, is typically reserved for older people for whom a fall is more likely to be a medical emergency. However, this phrase can be considered patronizing by those to whom it is applied.<ref>{{RQ:Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2022/jun/14/young-fall-over-older-people-stepmother-broke-knees|title=The young fall over, older people ‘have a fall’ – and my stepmother is none too happy about it|author=Zoe Williams|date=14 June 2022|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20261018094109/https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2022/jun/14/young-fall-over-older-people-stepmother-broke-knees|archivedate=18 October 2026|ascite=1}}</ref><ref>{{cite-web|titleurl=https://medium.com/crows-feet/are-we-talking-about-falls-the-wrong-way-9a41d9b3b410|title=Are We Talking About Falls The Wrong Way?|first=Janice|last=Harayada|date=12 November 2023|work=Crow's Feet|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20260201020829/https://medium.com/crows-feet/are-we-talking-about-falls-the-wrong-way-9a41d9b3b410|archivedate=1 February 2026}}</ref>
